description:
We are a systems engineer and an economist, contributing viable solutions for humanity.

We are looking for people with ideas on how to survive in the future—exploring new frontiers and the adaptation of human beings to new habitats beyond our planet.
summary:
For nearly five decades, iconic NASA missions—from Viking and Pathfinder to Opportunity, InSight, and Ingenuity—explored Mars and fell silent. Instead of seeing them as space junk, our team developed BLESS-Mars (Bioregenerative Life-Support Environmental Spirulina System), an 8-module hybrid habitat architecture and STEM storytelling program that gives this forgotten hardware a second life to keep future astronauts alive.

We address the challenge by pairing circular engineering with educational narrative. Technically, we repurpose titanium tanks from Viking and Sky Cranes for gas storage, Opportunity’s radioisotope heaters for night warmth, InSight’s solar arrays for lighting, and Ingenuity’s processors for edge computing—harmonized under NASA’s FAIRUST data principles. Biologically, four 650-liter Spirulina photobioreactors produce 35% of the crew’s oxygen (1.18 kg/day) and nutrient-rich food for four astronauts over 500 days.

Why does it matter? Reusing Martian hardware and local ice cuts mission launch mass (ESM) by 32% (saving 383.8 kg from hardware recycling alone) while teaching children that in space—and on Earth—nothing is wasted.
details:
1. PROJECT DETAILS

BLESS-Mars (Bioregenerative Life-Support Environmental Spirulina System) is an 8-module hybrid life-support architecture (M1–M8) and STEM educational program that transforms retired NASA hardware on Mars into an active oxygen, food, and data-governance hub. Instead of relying solely on heavy physicochemical systems launched from Earth, BLESS-Mars cultivates Arthrospira platensis (Spirulina) across four 650-liter photobioreactor loops (2.60 m³ total volume, 46.1 m² illuminated area). For a 4-person crew on a 500-day mission, the system produces 1.176 kg/day of oxygen (35.0% of metabolic demand), captures 1.520 kg/day of CO₂ (38.0% of crew output), and yields 0.871 kg/day of protein-rich biomass (435.5 kg total), while recycling 95% of process water.

To power and house this biological core, we repurpose hardware from seven historic NASA mission families: Viking 1 & 2 titanium pressure spheres for O₂/CO₂ buffer storage; Mars Pathfinder Vectran airbags for micrometeorite shielding; Spirit & Opportunity Pu-238 Radioisotope Heater Units (RHUs) for passive nocturnal heating (30–35 °C); Phoenix's titanium scoop arm and MECA electrochemical cells for subsurface ice extraction and nutrient monitoring; InSight's UltraFlex solar arrays and TWINS meteorology sensors for LED lighting and environmental telemetry; EDL/Sky Crane MLI thermal blankets and over 400 m² of Nylon/Kevlar parachutes for reactor insulation and washable electrostatic dust pre-filters; and Ingenuity's flight processor as a local Edge AI diagnostic node.

2. Key Benefits & Intended Impact

By combining Martian water In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) with Technological ISRU (reclaiming existing NASA hardware), BLESS-Mars cuts Equivalent System Mass (ESM) by 32.0% over 500 days—dropping from 2,491.5 kg (baseline physicochemical ECLSS) to 1,695.0 kg, with 383.8 kg saved directly from recycled spacecraft parts—and reaches 725.6 kg over a 1,095-day mission. Beyond astronaut survival, our 4-lesson STEM curriculum ("From Silent Explorers to Guardians of Life") uses these spacecraft stories to teach elementary students circular sustainability, biology, and space data literacy.

3. Tools, Software & Engineering Frameworks Used

- Modeling & Simulation: Python (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib) for coupled mass-energy balance equations, dynamic failure simulations across eight operating scenarios (S0–S7), and a 1,000-run Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis.

- Data Architecture: A three-tier Federated Data Governance Framework aligned with NASA's FY2025–FY2027 Data Strategy (NID 2800.149) and DAMA-DMBOK2, translating legacy 1976–2024 sensor outputs into open JSON-LD and HDF5 schemas under FAIRUST (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable, Understandable, Secure, Trustworthy) principles.

- Documentation & Educational Design: Technical architecture schematics, comparative ESM tables, and classroom storytelling guides.

4. Creativity & Factors Considered

Our core creative leap is treating silent rovers and landers not as space debris, but as an active spare-parts bank and educational cast—turning technical components into memorable characters for children (such as "Opportunity's Warm Heart" and "Viking's Grandparent Tanks"). Engineering factors rigorously evaluated include the 4-to-24-minute Earth–Mars communication latency (solved via autonomous Edge AI in Module M8), extreme nocturnal cold, Martian dust storms, radiation-induced sensor drift (mitigated via Triple Modular Redundancy with 2-of-3 voting in Module M6), and system resilience, maintaining an overall availability of A ≥ 0.915 (91.5%) even under severe multi-module failures.
